heading: The Prologue, John 1:1–18
lede: Which early manuscripts preserve each verse of John’s opening hymn, where they disagree, and which disagreements change how the passage is translated. Greek manuscripts up to AD 900 come first; early Latin manuscripts follow as a second layer.
scope: Greek papyri and majuscules to AD 900 (primary); key Latin manuscripts to AD 900 (secondary)
translation_note: Literal translation by the project, following the modern critical Greek text.

verses.translation: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
He was in the beginning with God.
All things came into being through him, and without him not one thing came into being.
verses.greek_where_variant: χωρὶς αὐτοῦ ἐγένετο οὐδὲ ἕν. ὃ γέγονεν

verses.translation: What has come into being in him was life, and the life was the light of humanity.
The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not overcome it.
There came a man, sent from God, whose name was John.
He came as a witness, to testify about the light, so that all might believe through him.
He was not the light, but came to testify about the light.
The true light, which enlightens every person, was coming into the world.
He was in the world, and the world came into being through him, yet the world did not know him.
He came to what was his own, and his own people did not receive him.
But to all who received him, who believed in his name, he gave power to become children of God,
who were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of a man, but of God.
And the Word became flesh and lived among us, and we have seen his glory, glory as of a father’s only son, full of grace and truth.
John testified about him and cried out, “This was he of whom I said, ‘He who comes after me ranks ahead of me, because he was before me.’”
From his fullness we have all received, grace upon grace.
For the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.
No one has ever seen God. The only-begotten God, who is close to the Father’s heart, has made him known.
verses.greek_where_variant: μονογενὴς θεὸς ὁ ὢν εἰς τὸν κόλπον τοῦ πατρός

variants.label: God / Son
variants.title: “The only-begotten God” or “the only-begotten Son”?

readings.witnesses: 02 · 04 (corrector) · 017 · 037 · 038 · 041 · 044 · most later Greek manuscripts · Latin tradition (unigenitus Filius) · Curetonian Syriac

variants.explanation: This is the variant in the Prologue that most changes translations: “God the only Son” (NRSV) or “the only God” (ESV) against “the only begotten Son” (KJV). The two earliest papyri and the two great 4th-century codices read θεός; υἱός has broad support from the 5th century on and matches the phrase “only-begotten Son” elsewhere in John (3:16, 18). Because the names were written as abbreviated ‘sacred names’ (ΘΣ and ΥΣ), the difference on the page is a single letter. The committee behind the modern critical text preferred θεός as the earlier and harder reading; Ehrman argued that θεός is a 2nd-century change made to stress Christ’s divinity against ‘adoptionist’ views.

variants.label: punctuation
variants.title: Where does the sentence end?

readings.greek: οὐδὲ ἕν. ὃ γέγονεν ἐν αὐτῷ ζωὴ ἦν
readings.english: …not one thing came into being. What has come into being in him was life.
readings.witnesses: stop before ὃ γέγονεν: 𝔓75 (corrector) · 04 · 05 · 019 · 032 (replacement quire) · 050 (first hand) · Irenaeus, Clement of Alexandria, Origen, Tertullian and most 2nd–3rd-century writers

readings.greek: οὐδὲ ἓν ὃ γέγονεν. ἐν αὐτῷ ζωὴ ἦν
readings.english: …not one thing that has come into being. In him was life.
readings.witnesses: stop after ὃ γέγονεν: many later manuscripts · most writers from the late 4th century on. No punctuation at all: 𝔓66 · 𝔓75 (first hand) · 01 (first hand) · 02 · 03 · 037

variants.explanation: The earliest manuscripts mostly have no punctuation, so the words are identical and only the pause differs. Early writers overwhelmingly read the first way. From the 4th century the second became dominant, partly because the first had been used in the Arian controversy and in arguments about whether the Holy Spirit was a created being. Kurt Aland argued that the early reading, joining ὃ γέγονεν to verse 4, is original; the Nestle–Aland text has printed it that way since its 26th edition. This is a case where the manuscripts, the early readers and later theology all bear on a translation choice.

variants.label: was / is
variants.title: “Was life” or “is life”?

readings.witnesses: 01 · 05 · Old Latin · some Vulgate manuscripts · Irenaeus (Latin) · Heracleon · Clement and Origen (in part)

variants.explanation: The present tense may have come from reading the previous words (ὃ γέγονεν, “what has come into being”) with this clause, which makes “is” sound more natural. A small change, but a good example of Sinaiticus and Bezae agreeing against the other early witnesses.

variants.label: who / he who
variants.title: “Who were born” or “he who was born”?

readings.witnesses: Old Latin Codex Veronensis (b) · some Syriac manuscripts · Irenaeus and Tertullian (2nd–3rd c.)

variants.explanation: No Greek manuscript has the singular, but it was read by 2nd- and 3rd-century writers and survives in a 5th-century Latin manuscript. In the singular the verse becomes a statement about Jesus’s birth ‘not of blood … nor of the will of a man’, which is why it matters to readers interested in early ideas about the virgin birth. It is also the clearest reason this site keeps a Latin layer.

translation_sweep.question: “The Word was God”, “a god”, or “divine”?
translation_sweep.explanation: The manuscripts agree; the debate is grammatical. Here θεός has no article and stands before the verb. Colwell (1933) observed that definite predicate nouns placed before the verb usually lack the article, which leaves room for “God”. Harner (1973) argued that such nouns are chiefly qualitative, stressing what the Word is, which is why some translations use “divine” or “what God was”. “A god” is the reading of a minority of translations. This will be treated in full in the translation sweep.
